items.title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I talked with the engineer and Bob Weinstein who was the guy who owned the company... So I said, 'Well what’s his name?' He said, 'Rudy Vangelder.' So I go over to Rudy’s studio prior to recording... And we sat and talked about piano, Rudy and I.

ctx.x: Did you find working with Prestege any better than the other previous record labels or was it pretty much business as usual?

No, Prestege was the first label that I worked with where I was allowed to play what I wanted to. As a matter of fact the first record that I made for Prestege I talked with the engineer and Bob Weinstein who was the guy who owned the company had only recorded Lenny Testrano prior to that. And I didn’t like the sound that he got on Lenny. I had heard Lenny play and I said, “You know when I listen to Lenny he gets a deeper… it’s another sound that he gets that I like better.” I said, “Where are we going to…

Savoy thing, it was a B but it wasn’t… it hadn’t been well kept and it didn’t sound as good as Rudy Vangelder made those pianos sound. So we went over… we listened to these things and with his engineer’s ear he heard certain things and that became the Rudy Vangelder sound. So the piano sound that I get on… that he got on me, on these first records was his point of reference for all of the sound. And what is interesting to me when other pianist who sounded quite different from me in person, would go and record for…
